---
title: Performance
description: "Control work through branch limits, feed the device, tune batch size, and compile selected regions."
---

Measure the complete workload: source reading and preprocessing, tensorization,
model computation, and prediction writing. Schema shape and requested outputs
can matter as much as model width. Compare quality and throughput under the
same data, hardware, precision, and optimization budget.

## Define the measurement

Training throughput counts training observations processed per elapsed second;
inference throughput counts observations whose selected outputs have been
produced per second. State the timing boundary: a model-compute rate and an
end-to-end rate include different work. For an end-to-end rate, include source
reading, preprocessing, encoding, device completion, and output writing where
applicable. Report HTTP requests per second separately when a request can
contain multiple observations.

One observation can contain many transactions, nested purchases, and prediction
targets. Report retained record counts and active target positions as well as
observation counts, so a change in nested shape is visible in the comparison.
Record these conditions alongside any measured rate:

| Condition | What to report |
| --- | --- |
| Workload | Task, source format, record count, schema depth, retained collection-length distribution and caps, and target counts at each depth. |
| Model and output | Resolved architecture, vocabulary sizes, selected predictions and representations, and output format. |
| Hardware and runtime | CPU and accelerator models, device count and memory, precision, package versions, and compilation mode. |
| Batching | Observations per device, worker count, gradient accumulation for training, and concurrency or microbatching for HTTP serving. |
| Timing | Warmup, accelerator synchronization, timed stages, and whether validation, checkpointing, compilation, and startup are included. |

Compare task quality alongside throughput under the same protocol. A rate
measured for one schema and machine establishes performance for that workload;
use [recorded evidence](../evidence.qmd) with its stated conditions when
making a measured claim.

## Control work first

Repeated branches use the largest retained collection length in each batch.
The default `length=None` retains all slots; a finite limit bounds retention
and permits an overflow policy. Even bounded branches compact their internal
width below the cap when possible. Nested batch maxima can multiply coordinate
counts. Choose limits that retain the context the task needs; reductions
determine how much reaches the parent. These choices also affect model quality.
See [Branch](../datatypes/branch.qmd#automatic-lengths-and-limits).

Padding and structurally skipped coordinates are absent from attention.
Eligible encoder work packs present coordinates when the layers have no
customizations or active stochastic dropout. This is automatic; it does not
require changing the input schema. Null and learned-mask coordinates remain
present model inputs.

Padding is not free. Dense embedding buffers, concatenation, unpacking, and
learned pooling still consume memory. Packed attention operates on real
sequences, whose pairwise work grows quadratically with their lengths. One long
record can dominate a batch even when its neighbors are short. Set finite
limits for untrusted inputs.

On CUDA, eligible encoder sequences with every coordinate present omit padding
masks, allowing PyTorch to select native FlashAttention. The same presence
check chooses between this path and packing; no extra device synchronization is
needed. Active stochastic dropout, custom implementations, and hooks retain
their ordinary contracts. Oversized sequence batches retain masks to respect
the native FlashAttention batch limit.

Export only needed outputs. Root or branch embeddings, repeated leaf outputs,
and Category top-k values enlarge the prediction payload. Selecting a larger
batch can improve utilization but also changes updates per epoch; account for
that when comparing training runs.

## Let Lightning select training hardware

`model.fit(...)` selects available hardware by default: `accelerator="auto"`,
`devices="auto"`, DDP with unused-parameter detection for multiple devices, and
BF16 mixed precision where the selected devices support it. Otherwise it uses
FP32. Override these choices only when the workload needs it; see
[Training options](training-options.qmd#choose-the-loop).

BF16 mixed precision keeps neural parameters in float32 while eligible
computation uses BF16. Number source values, normalization statistics, and
source-unit readout stay float64 on CPU and CUDA, outside mixed precision;
Apple MPS uses float32 because it has no float64 support. See
[Number precision](../datatypes/number.qmd). When using `lit.Trainer` directly,
configure its hardware and precision explicitly; it does not inherit the
model-method defaults.

On a single-device machine, add Lightning's native `BatchSizeFinder` to tune
`model.batch_size` before training. `ArrowDataModule.batch_size` reads and
writes that same value, and rebuilt loaders use the selected size. The
example uses the [transaction-history model](../learn/add-transaction-history.qmd)
as `model` and application-supplied training and validation Parquet files:

```python
from lightning.pytorch.callbacks import BatchSizeFinder
import relflow as rf

datamodule = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="payments/history/train.parquet",
    validate="payments/history/validation.parquet",
)
finder = BatchSizeFinder(mode="binsearch", steps_per_trial=3, max_val=64)
model.fit(datamodule, fused=None, devices=1, callbacks=[finder], max_epochs=20)
```

`fused=None` delegates AdamW implementation selection to Torch, including on
MPS. The finder restores its temporary checkpoint before the real fit;
`finder.optimal_batch_size` reports its selected size.

The finder does not support distributed strategies. On a multi-GPU machine,
`devices="auto"` normally selects all visible GPUs, so tune on one device
first with Lightning's `Tuner` (which uses `BatchSizeFinder` internally),
then train with automatic device count and no finder callback. The native
Trainer probe needs an explicit optimizer factory. This CUDA example assumes
BF16 support for both the probe and the real fit:

```python
import lightning.pytorch as lit
from lightning.pytorch.tuner import Tuner

model.optimizer = rf.adamw(learning_rate=1e-3, fused=None)
tuning = lit.Trainer(accelerator="auto", devices=1, precision="bf16-mixed")
Tuner(tuning).scale_batch_size(
    model, datamodule=datamodule, mode="binsearch", max_val=64,
)
model.optimizer = None
model.fit(datamodule, max_epochs=20)
```

The probe's optimizer assignment is cleared before the ordinary fit, which
configures its own optimization for the current model.

Keep a conservative cap and supply enough representative records to fill the
candidate batches, including dense histories and participating targets.
Lightning's finder is a short capacity heuristic, not a throughput benchmark
or a guarantee for unseen records, later vocabulary growth, or DDP overhead.
Its `margin` reduces the selected batch in binsearch mode; it is not a GPU
memory reservation. Lightning temporarily disables callbacks during its probes,
so extension callbacks that allocate additional state still need a real-fit
smoke test. A cap reached during the search is not necessarily itself probed.

Retune when HPO changes model shape, context lengths, precision, or optimizer.
The nominal effective batch is the batch size multiplied by the device count
and gradient-accumulation count on one node; set accumulation explicitly when
comparing trials, and account for incomplete final accumulation windows.

## Feed the device

Loop `batch_size` overrides set the model's current encoded batch size, for
example `model.fit(datamodule, batch_size=128, max_epochs=30)`. The value is per
device under DDP. Loader settings belong on the data module; tune them after
measuring whether input preparation leaves the device idle:

```python
datamodule = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="payments/history/train.parquet",
    validate="payments/history/validation.parquet",
    num_workers=4,
    persistent_workers=True,
    pin_memory=True,
    prefetch_factor=2,
)
```

Workers and prefetching consume host memory. Arrow sources and retained data
remain on CPU while encoded tensors move to the model's device. Local data
workers divide the source before preprocessing: file sources split their
manifests so each worker reads only its files, streams are still read by every
worker but each keeps alternate units, and in-memory tables stride rows. Each
worker then preprocesses, samples, shuffles, and encodes only its share.
Distributed ranks replay the source before disjoint row selection, so adding
ranks does not reduce source I/O. Keep Arrow/Polars transformations columnar
instead of repeatedly converting observations to Python rows.

Throughput uses the actual number of observations in each Arrow or TensorDict
batch, including a partial final batch. Other custom batch types fall back to
the configured model batch size. It measures elapsed host time around batch
processing.
It logs with `on_step=True, on_epoch=False`. `throughput/train` reaches attached
loggers every `log_every_n_steps` optimizer updates; validation, test, and
prediction throughput are reported per batch. With gradient accumulation, the
training rate describes the latest microbatch. Timing excludes input loading
and encoding before the batch start hook. Rates remain per rank and do not wait for CUDA work
to complete; they are not an end-to-end or synchronized GPU benchmark.
Compare runs with the same batch geometry and measure application loading,
encoding, device completion, and writing separately when reporting throughput.
Prediction throughput is retained by the callback and
sent directly to attached loggers; it is not a `trainer.callback_metrics` result.

## Configure AdamW {#use-the-adamw-factory}

```python
model.fit(datamodule, learning_rate=1e-4, weight_decay=0.01, fused=True, max_epochs=30)
```

Ordinary fits default to fused Torch AdamW. Use `fused=False` for an unsupported
device or `fused=None` for Torch's selection. Biases, scalar and one-dimensional
parameters, and names containing `"norm"` receive no weight decay by default.
See [Optimization](training-options.qmd#configure-optimization-and-callbacks) for all
options and per-run state. When resuming, keep optimizer settings consistent
with the saved run.

## Compile encoder and pool regions

`model.compile()` updates the existing model and returns it, so it can follow
a constructor or be called programmatically before training or inference.

```python
model.compile()
model.compile(encoders=True, pools=False)
model.compile(encoders=False, pools=True)
model.compile(encoders=False, pools=False)
```

Each call replaces the previous selection. The last call above restores eager
execution.

| Switch | Selected region |
| --- | --- |
| `encoders=True` | Branch sequence encoder stacks. |
| `pools=True` | Learned attention reductions in branches and decoders. |

Coordinate encoders, routing, tensorfield operations, mean pooling, losses,
metrics, and optimizer execution keep their ordinary paths. Each selected
dense region uses `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)`. Packed grouping and its
grouped encoder execution stay eager so changing batch composition does not
create a compiler specialization for every group layout. Custom compute
implementations remain eager, as do customized regions and regions with
nested hooks, including hooks added after compilation.

```python
model.compile(backend="inductor", dynamic=True, options={})
```

`backend="inductor"`, `dynamic=None`, and `options=None` are the defaults.
Omitting `dynamic`, or passing `None`, enables dynamic shapes; `True` also
enables them and `False` specializes shapes. Inductor defaults preserve eager
random draws and disable CUDA graphs and automatic tensor padding.
Backend-specific `options` override those defaults. Floating-point results can
still differ.

Compilation happens lazily on real inputs. Measure initial compilation and
steady-state execution separately, covering the batch sizes, branch occupancy,
training mode, and inference mode used by the application. Compilation is not
a guaranteed speedup: first establish a useful result on representative work.
Compiler errors in selected regions propagate rather than silently selecting
an eager fallback.

Schema mutations, checkpoint rebuilds, and model copies do not preserve
compilation. Reapply it after loading or changing the model. Compilation is
not stored in checkpoints.
